tagline: A lift bridge and mine shafthouses mark the road to Copper Harbor.
intro: US 41 climbs Quincy Hill above Hancock before following the center of the Keweenaw Peninsula through Calumet toward Phoenix. The Copper Country Trail organization presents this National Byway as a journey through mining history and the peninsula’s natural features. The Federal Highway Administration’s archived description gives 47 miles and an hour for a one-way drive, with historic downtowns and mine shafthouses carrying the story.

Congress authorized a military wagon road in 1863, providing a land connection when ice or storms stopped Great Lakes transport. The 1864 layout followed today’s US 41 between Houghton and Phoenix, then today’s M-26 toward Copper Harbor. The wagon road was poorly built and barely passable except when the ground froze or snow covered it; nearby railroads attracted more traffic. US 41 received its number in 1926; national byway designation followed in 2005.

Begin in Houghton, cross the Portage Lake Lift Bridge to Hancock and climb past Quincy Mine. Continue through Calumet to Phoenix, where US 41 turns east through Central and Delaware. At Copper Harbor, Brockway Mountain Drive is a separate loop off M-26, with twists, hills and sharp hairpins. US 41 itself continues past Fort Wilkins State Park to a cul-de-sac marked by a wooden sign.

moments.title: Portage Lake Lift Bridge
moments.text: The bridge between Houghton and Hancock was designed to carry both roads and rails on its movable span. Partly raising the span let smaller boats pass underneath without stopping vehicles; trains required the span to be lowered. The present bridge replaced a swing bridge in 1959. Rail service ended in 1982, changing how the two decks were used. In winter, after the lake freezes, the span is lowered so snowmobiles can use the bottom deck. The crossing is the only land link between the northern and southern sections of the Keweenaw Peninsula.

moments.title: Quincy Mine
moments.text: Quincy’s No. 2 shaft followed the copper deposit for 9,260 feet on a 55-degree slope, reaching 6,200 feet vertically below its entrance. A steam hoist built in 1918 raised and lowered ore and workers along that shaft. Its elaborate hoist house served as a showpiece for visiting investors. Despite the investment, the steam hoist was used for only eleven years, ending in 1929. Since mining stopped, groundwater has filled the workings up to the seventh level. A drainage tunnel keeps that level clear; Michigan Tech enlarged the tunnel in the 1970s for a mining study.

moments.title: Brockway Mountain Drive
moments.text: Low stone walls line Brockway Mountain Drive as it climbs the Keweenaw Fault’s ridge above Lake Superior. The county road commission began construction in 1933 with federal funding to employ copper miners left jobless by the Depression. Workers graded the road by hand, assisted by horses. The road opened in October 1933, with work on its stone walls continuing the following year. The route reaches 720 feet above the lake, with viewpoints over Copper Harbor, Lake Superior and undeveloped woodland. Toward Copper Harbor, two sharp hairpins lead into the descent from the ridge.

practical: Brockway Mountain Drive: Brockway Mountain Drive is not plowed and is closed to cars in winter, when it serves as a snowmobile trail. (checked 2026-10-11)
